concepts.name: Dunder methods and the data model

questions.prompt: In `with open(path) as f: ...`, when is the file's `__exit__` method called?

choices.text: Only when the block finishes without an error
Whenever the block exits, including when an exception is raised

questions.explanation: `__exit__` always runs when the block is left, whether it finishes normally, returns early or raises. That is what makes `with` reliable for cleanup.

questions.prompt: What happens when `__exit__` returns `True` after an exception was raised inside the `with` block?

choices.text: The exception is suppressed and execution continues after the block

questions.explanation: A truthy return value from `__exit__` tells Python the exception has been handled, so it is swallowed. Suppress only what you mean to, as `contextlib.suppress` does.

questions.prompt: In a function decorated with `@contextlib.contextmanager`, when does the code after `yield` run?

choices.text: When the `with` block exits, but only on error unless it is in a `finally`
Every time the block accesses the yielded value

questions.explanation: The code before `yield` is setup and the code after it is teardown. If the block raises, the exception is raised at the `yield` point, so teardown only runs if it sits in a `finally` (or you catch the exception).

questions.prompt: Describe a `timer()` context manager built with `contextlib.contextmanager` that logs elapsed milliseconds. Why does `try`/`finally` matter here?

model_answer.summary: Record the start time, yield inside `try`, and compute and log the elapsed time in `finally`, so the timing is logged even when the block raises.
key_points: Record the start with `time.perf_counter()` before the `yield`
In `finally`, compute the elapsed milliseconds and log them
`finally` guarantees the log line even if the block raises, and the exception still propagates to the caller

questions.explanation: Timing and tracing helpers like this are how you measure latency per step in an agent. Without `finally`, a failing call records no timing at all, which is exactly the case you most want to see.

questions.prompt: Which method makes `len(obj)` work on your class?
questions.explanation: Built-in functions call dunder methods: `len()` calls `__len__`, `repr()` calls `__repr__`, and `obj[i]` calls `__getitem__`. Implementing them makes your objects work like built-in types.

questions.prompt: A class defines `__eq__` but not `__hash__`. What happens to its instances?

choices.text: They become unhashable, because `__hash__` is set to `None`
Python raises an error when the class is defined
They hash by the result of `__eq__`

questions.explanation: Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes. Python can't guarantee that for a custom `__eq__`, so it sets `__hash__` to `None`. Define `__hash__` consistently, or use a frozen dataclass.

questions.prompt: What happens when you assign to a field of a `@dataclass(frozen=True)` instance?

choices.text: A new instance is created automatically

questions.explanation: Frozen dataclasses block attribute assignment after `__init__`. To change a value, create a new instance, for example with `dataclasses.replace`.

questions.prompt: Why does a dataclass list field need `field(default_factory=list)`? What does `frozen=True` give you for a record like token `Usage`?

model_answer.summary: A plain list default would be shared by every instance, so dataclasses reject it; `default_factory` builds a new list for each instance. Frozen instances can't change, so they are safe to share and can be hashed.
key_points: A mutable default would be shared by every instance, the same bug as mutable default arguments
Dataclasses refuse a bare `list`, `dict` or `set` default and raise `ValueError`
`default_factory=list` creates a new list for each instance
`frozen=True` makes instances immutable, so they are safe to pass around and hashable; you combine usage records with `__add__` returning a new instance

questions.explanation: Immutable value objects remove a whole class of shared-state bugs. That matters in async agent code, where many tasks handle the same records.
